21.reason: To jangle someone's nerves is glossed in standard dictionaries both as to irritate someone (Merriam-Webster: to excite to tense irritation) and as to make someone nervous or upset (Cambridge, Collins). The first gloss points to annoy (B) and the second to disturb (C), and both are fair interpretations of the idiom. Codex's case that disturb is too general has force, but so does the case that annoy misses the unsettling, nervous element. Harass and tease wrongly add deliberate, repeated provocation. A well-prepared student cannot tell whether the setter wanted B or C, so no key should be forced.
